name: Rafael Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential. Could you take me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior operator on one of the forming machines at Ardent Glass, which makes bottles and jars. The furnace never goes out, so we run round the clock, and I'm on the day crew from 6 to 2. My job is to keep the machine's moulds timed right, watch the gob of glowing glass drop and swap sections when a mould wears out. When it's running right, there's nothing like the sight of a thousand bottles an hour coming off the line.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the fire and the rhythm, and I love that a bottle I make might end up on a family's Sunday table. What wears me out is the heat, the noise, and the burns on my forearms that never fully heal. And the early start, but I like an early start, so I can't complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fine, and probably about right. I'd tell the lads on the crew that the tools are useful, use them and move on. I'd tell the church group that the world doesn't end every time a new machine arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a little bored. I like a challenge, and I've already got a plan for the next few years. My job carries on, so I'd carry on with my plan, which is to start a small repair business with my son Emil when I retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running my machine and keep using the AI tool to read the mould-wear charts and write my shift reports. I'd put 250 a month into the plan for the workshop and keep going with the evening class in welding that I started. And I'd pay my share to the church building fund, which I always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, even. Steady and clear, with room for projects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools every day already. What for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I ask the assistant to explain the vendor's error codes in plain words, and I check what it says against my own eyes. It also helps me spot patterns in the reject logs and write my handover notes. That saves me half an hour a day, which I use to walk the line and talk to the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is the money, and what's on your mind at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We're comfortable, not rich. My wife Tereza teaches at a primary school, and we have about four months of savings. Our daughter Zora is a pharmacist and our son Emil is a mechanical technician, so the kids are settled and we don't worry about them.

say: I'd tell the crew the tools are **useful**, so use them and move on.
The world doesn't end every time a **new machine** arrives.
think: I'd be a little **bored**, since my job carries on and my plan is already in motion.
My plan is a small **repair business** with my son Emil after retirement.
do: Keep running my machine and use AI to read **mould-wear charts** and write handover notes.
Put **250 a month** towards the workshop plan.
Keep going to the evening **welding class**.
feel: **Good** and steady, with room for projects.
S0.quote: I ask the assistant to explain
fieldNote: **Plan already running**: AI at work, welding class in the evening, savings for a workshop.
**Checks the tool** against his own eyes, a sign of adaptive but careful use.
**Family settled**, which frees money and energy for the business plan.

steps.text: Keep running the forming machine and write handover notes with AI
Put 250 a month into the workshop fund
Keep going to the evening welding class
Stay on the day crew until retirement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what I've been preparing for. I'd tell the crew that change is coming, and it's best to meet it with a skill in your hand and a plan in your head. I'd say the people who do their jobs well and learn a little each year will be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I think my job gets better. The software takes over the planning and checks, and I stay on the machine, because robots are slower to come to hot, messy work like ours. I'd also be the one explaining the new systems to the older operators, which I'd enjoy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Ardent to put me on the new predictive-maintenance project, and I'd finish my welding certificate to add a trade. I'd start looking at a used workshop lathe for the repair business with Emil. And I'd put another 150 a month into the workshop fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, a bit of excitement. I like the feeling of being ahead of the curve, even at 58.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks at Ardent Glass are the thinking tasks that software would take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The schedule planning, the order sheets, the quality reports and the maintenance calendar. The plant already uses software for some of it, and the assistant does the rest in minutes. On the floor, cameras watch the bottle shapes. A person still has to fix a jam in a mould at 1,000 degrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your church friends see all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of them would say be careful, don't throw away what's proven. I'd say yes, and also learn the new thing. We're allowed to value old ways and still learn a new tool, and I think that's what a good tradesman does.

say: I'd tell the crew to meet change with a **skill in your hand** and a plan in your head.
People who learn **a little each year** will be fine.
think: My job gets **better**, as software takes planning and robots are slower to reach hot, messy work.
I'd enjoy explaining the new systems to the **older operators**.
do: Ask to join the **predictive-maintenance** project at Ardent.
Finish my **welding certificate** to add a trade.
Look at a used **workshop lathe** for the repair business and save 150 a month more.
feel: **Good**, with excitement at being ahead of the curve even at 58.
S1.quote: A person still has to fix a jam
fieldNote: **Moves first** and sees change as a chance to add trades to his name.
**Traditional and open**: values old ways but says a good tradesman learns new tools.
**Business plan** with his son gets more concrete in this picture.

steps.text: Ask to join the plant's predictive-maintenance project
Finish the welding certificate at night school
Look at a used workshop lathe for the repair business
Save another 150 a month for the workshop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to stay calm and get to work, today. I'd tell the crew that Ardent needs to tell us what its plan is, and that the church and the families need to help each other. Two years is short, but not impossible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be worried, and I'd say so. The thinking work goes in 2028, and the plant might cut a lot of its office and planning staff. I'd have about three more years on the machine before the robots come to the line, but the furnace is expensive to run, and a bad year could mean closure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Tereza that night and cut our spending by a quarter. I'd bring the workshop plan forward and look at buying the lathe within a year, so that Emil and I could start earlier. I'd take extra courses on the plant's automation system, and I'd ask to be the person who looks after the robots when they come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense. I'd be restless and I'd probably burn a few extra hours in the garage making things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come about 2031. Is hot, messy work really protected until then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly. Glass is hot, heavy, messy work and robots will find it hard to handle at first. But the planning and maintenance side goes in 2028. I'd count the three years as a maybe, not a promise, because Ardent could shut a furnace if the numbers change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter Zora that pharmacies will still need people, and to learn the AI tools that check prescriptions. I'd tell my son Emil it's time to start our business together, because the best insurance is something of your own. And I'd tell them both we have a plan and God has the rest.

say: I'd say stay **calm**, get to work, and the plant must tell us its plan.
Two years is short, but **not impossible**.
think: I'd be **worried**, because the plant might cut planning staff and a bad year could close it.
I'd count the three years before robots as a **maybe**.
do: Talk to Tereza and cut spending by **a quarter**.
Bring the **workshop plan** forward and buy the lathe within a year.
Take the plant's **automation courses** and ask to look after the robots.
feel: **Tense** and restless, burning extra hours in the garage making things.
fieldNote: **Adaptive action**: he brings the business plan forward rather than waiting.
**Faith in the plan**: he trusts preparation and says God has the rest.
**Uneasy, not anxious**, because the skills and the business plan give him some control.

steps.text: Cut household spending by a quarter with Tereza
Buy the used lathe within a year
Start the repair business with Emil on weekends
Take the plant's automation courses and offer to look after robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a gift, if we use it. I'd say it to the crew and the church group, that five years is enough to get a trade and put something by. I'd also say there's no excuse for waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine. AI arrives when I'm 63 and robots at 66, and by then I'd be retired and running the workshop with Emil. What I'd feel is a sense of responsibility for the younger operators, who have more to lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the welding certificate, buy the lathe in the first year and take on small jobs on weekends. I'd save 400 a month towards the business and a cushion of eight months. And I'd help two of the younger operators learn the maintenance side, so they have more than one string to their bow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. I'd feel I've been given enough time to do it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, what do you do differently from the two-year plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be in a hurry. With five I can start the business slowly and not borrow big. A man of 58 shouldn't be in debt at 63.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair rules and good apprenticeships, and don't tax people into the ground. Give a tax break to firms that train their workers and keep them on. And don't hand out money in place of work, because people need purpose as well as pay.

say: I'd say five years is a **gift**, enough to get a trade and put something by.
think: I'd be fine, since I'd be **retired** and running the workshop with Emil by 2034.
I feel **responsible** for the younger operators, who have more to lose.
do: Finish the **welding certificate**, buy the lathe in year one and take weekend jobs.
Save **400 a month** towards the business and an eight-month cushion.
Teach two younger operators the **maintenance** side.
feel: **Good**, with enough time to do it right.
fieldNote: **A slow start** lets him avoid borrowing, which fits his cautious side.
**Policy view**: fair rules, apprenticeships and tax breaks for firms that keep workers.

steps.text: Finish the welding certificate and buy the lathe in year one
Buy the used lathe without borrowing a large sum
Save 400 a month for the business and cushion
Take small repair jobs on weekends with Emil

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big blessing, a whole decade to get ready. I'd say it at the plant and at church, that it's the right time to plant seeds, whether that's a trade or a small business. A decade is plenty if you start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's easy. I'd be retired well before 2039, and the repair business would be a few years old. I think about the young people, mostly, and my grandchildren. It's their world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until 62 and then turn the garage workshop into a proper small business with Emil. I'd keep up with the AI tools so I can quote jobs and manage the books. And I'd keep putting a bit into savings, as I like to have a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and glad. I like the idea of ten years of building something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is long. Do you change anything about how you live?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, honestly. I'd carry on, and just stay curious. The thing I'd change is that I'd start the business a bit earlier, since there's no reason to wait if the plan is good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell somebody starting out in glass?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn the furnace and the machine, and learn the software that runs them. Be someone who can fix things and explain things. Treat your crew like family, because they'll be there when the work changes.

say: I'd say it's a **big blessing**, a whole decade to get ready.
It's the right time to **plant seeds**, whether that's a trade or a small business.
think: For me it's **easy**: I'd be retired before 2039 with the repair business a few years old.
I think about the **young people** and my grandchildren, because it's their world.
do: Work until **62**, then turn the garage into a proper small business with Emil.
Keep up with **AI tools** to quote jobs and manage the books.
Keep putting a little into **savings** for a cushion.
feel: **Calm and glad**, liking the idea of ten years of building something.
fieldNote: **Calm for real reasons**: long runway, plan in motion and adaptable habits.
**Wants to start earlier**, the only thing he'd change.
**Advice to youth** mixes machine skill, software and treating a crew like family.

steps.text: Work until 62, then open the repair business with Emil
Use AI tools to quote jobs and keep the books
Keep adding to savings as a cushion
Retire from the plant at 62

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, though I'd cope better than most. It's a race against the plant's own decisions, and I'd have no time to start the business slowly. What would help is paid training, a fair early-retirement route, and tax rules that don't punish a small firm for starting.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what a man owes the people who come after him. My father taught me glass, and I'll teach the young ones what I know. That's worth more than any gadget.

portrait: **Rafael** is a 58-year-old forming-machine operator at a glass container plant, with a faith-centred, family-minded outlook.
He uses **AI every day**, checks it with his own eyes, and plans a repair workshop with his son.
He has about **four months** of savings and settled grown-up children, so he can spend on his plan.
He is calm in most pictures and only **uneasy** in the two-year world, where the plant's choices decide his timing.
biggestWorry: The **two-year scenario**, because it leaves no time to start the business slowly.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training**, a fair early-retirement route and tax rules that don't punish a small firm for starting.
